idiom_name: frozen value objects (Data.define / freeze) with non-bang Enumerable methods
implementation_notes: Ruby has runtime enforcement that most languages lack: freeze makes any later mutation raise FrozenError, Data.define (Ruby 3.2) defines value-alike classes with readers and no writers at all, and the frozen_string_literal magic comment freezes literals file-wide so string constants cannot be changed in place. The naming convention carries the query/command split: a bang method mutates its receiver while its non-bang counterpart returns a new object (sort vs sort!, map vs map!), so queries use the non-bang forms and commands are the explicit bang exceptions. Freezing is shallow, so nested arrays and hashes must be frozen too or converted into frozen values.
code_sketch:
Money = Data.define(:amount, :currency) do
  def scaled(factor) = Money.new(amount * factor, currency)   # readers only, no writers
end

TOTAL = ->(lines) { lines.sum { |l| l.amount * l.qty } }      # query, mutates nothing
pitfalls: freeze is shallow: a frozen hash or array still holds mutable objects, so nested values must be frozen as well.
The bang convention is only a convention - libraries may violate it - so verify the implementation instead of trusting the name.
Instance-variable memoisation (@x ||= ...) raises FrozenError on a frozen object; compute in the constructor or in a companion object instead.
